paragraphs: When observations arrive in batches, corruption can affect whole groups of data rather than isolated examples. Some batches may even be chosen adversarially. This paper develops a general framework for learning under that kind of contamination, extending a setting previously studied for estimating distributions over finite collections of outcomes.

The framework covers both distribution estimation and classification on arbitrary domains, including continuous ones. Its agnostic formulation addresses learning without requiring a perfect fit to the chosen model family. For structured distributions, the authors derive polynomial-time robust estimation algorithms covering piecewise-polynomial, monotone, log-concave, and Gaussian-mixture families, while also improving the number of samples required.

For classification, the paper establishes near-optimal sample requirements and provides computationally efficient algorithms for interval-based classification. Intervals make this a particularly relevant case for one-dimensional prediction problems. The contribution combines limits on what learning can achieve with algorithms that approach those limits, showing how robustness to corrupted batches can extend across several distinct learning tasks.
neurips-2020-a-general-method-for-robust.tldr: A general framework yields robust distribution estimation and classification algorithms when some data batches are corrupted or adversarial.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover a rank-one matrix when only some entries are visible and an unknown subset of those entries has been corrupted. The corruptions can be arbitrarily large, so recovery cannot rely on every observed value being approximately correct. This mathematical problem becomes the foundation for a method that combines labels from potentially adversarial crowd workers.

The proposed algorithm combines alternating minimization with extreme-value filtering. The authors establish sufficient and necessary conditions for recovering the original matrix, and show that their algorithm is optimal when the pattern of revealed entries follows an Erdős–Rényi random graph. That optimality claim is tied to this stated observation model.

For crowdsourced classification, the majority of workers are assumed to answer correctly with worker-specific probabilities under a single-coin model. Other workers may behave arbitrarily, including deliberately trying to mislead the algorithm. Experiments show that the resulting matrix-completion approach outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods in this adversarial setting, supporting its usefulness when ordinary worker-noise assumptions fail for part of the crowd.
neurips-2020-adversarial-crowdsourcing-t.tldr: Robust rank-one matrix completion provides a way to combine crowd labels even when some workers deliberately supply misleading answers.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning uses knowledge from known classes to recognize classes without training examples. This paper focuses on visual attributes as the bridge between them. Its central proposal is that an image representation should capture both which attributes are present and where their visual evidence appears, making attribute knowledge more useful for transfer.

The framework learns global and local features together using only attributes supplied at the class level. A visual-semantic embedding layer learns global information, while an attribute prototype network learns local information from intermediate features. That network jointly predicts attributes and decorrelates them, encouraging the representation to distinguish attributes rather than treating them as an inseparable collection.

The resulting representations achieve state-of-the-art results on three zero-shot learning benchmarks in the reported evaluation. They also identify image regions that provide evidence for attributes, with examples on the CUB dataset. The findings connect improved recognition with improved attribute localization: the same representation supports transfer to unfamiliar classes and makes the visual basis of its attribute descriptions more visible.
neurips-2020-attribute-prototype-network.tldr: An attribute prototype network jointly learns global features and localized attribute evidence to improve zero-shot recognition.

paragraphs: This paper uses tensor decomposition to study why over-parameterized optimization can benefit from moving beyond lazy training. The task is to represent an order-l tensor with dimension d and rank r using m components, where the underlying rank is much smaller than the dimension and m exceeds r. Extra components provide flexibility during optimization.

The authors prove a large requirement for a lazy training regime analogous to the neural tangent kernel regime in neural networks: m must be at least on the order of d raised to l minus one. They then show that a variant of gradient descent can approximate the tensor using m = O*(r^(2.5l) log d), giving a substantially different dependence on dimension and rank.

This comparison demonstrates that over-parameterized gradient-based optimization can exploit low-rank structure beyond what the studied lazy regime permits. The result concerns approximate tensor recovery by a particular gradient-descent variant. Its broader significance is to provide a concrete setting where analysis beyond lazy training reveals capabilities that a lazy-regime description would miss.
neurips-2020-beyond-lazy-training-for-ov.tldr: A tensor-decomposition analysis shows that a gradient-descent variant can exploit low-rank structure with fewer components than lazy training requires.

paragraphs: Repeated interactions often come with information about the circumstances of each round. This paper formalizes contextual games, in which that information helps describe the game being played. The learning problem is to use relationships between contexts and outcomes so that each player can improve decisions across changing circumstances.

The authors express those relationships through kernel-based regularity assumptions and propose an online meta-algorithm that minimizes contextual regret. Regret measures the opportunity lost relative to better context-dependent choices. Sharing information across correlated contexts matters because experience under one set of circumstances can then inform decisions under another, rather than treating every context as unrelated.

The paper also defines contextual coarse correlated equilibria and optimal contextual welfare. It shows that these outcomes can be approached when players' contextual regrets vanish, making the conclusion conditional on that learning behavior. A traffic-routing experiment supports the framework empirically: exploiting context and its correlations produces better performance and higher welfare than the tested alternatives that leave that information unused.
neurips-2020-contextual-games-multi-agen.tldr: Contextual games connect learning from side information with equilibrium and welfare guarantees when players' contextual regrets vanish.

paragraphs: Vision systems can struggle when asked to recognize new classes or operate in a new domain using very few examples. This paper identifies supervision collapse as one reason: a representation may discard information unnecessary for its training task even when that information would help on a later task. Good performance on the original task therefore does not ensure useful transfer.

The authors propose two complementary remedies. Self-supervised learning encourages features with broader usefulness. CrossTransformers then compares an unlabeled query with a small set of labeled images by finding coarse spatial correspondences. Classification uses distances between features at corresponding locations, allowing the comparison to account for where relevant visual content appears.

The reported result is greater robustness to changes in both tasks and domains, supported by state-of-the-art performance on Meta-Dataset. That benchmark evaluates transfer from ImageNet to multiple other vision datasets. The contribution combines preserving transferable information during representation learning with a spatially aware comparison mechanism when only a few labeled examples are available.
neurips-2020-crosstransformers-spatially.tldr: CrossTransformers improve few-shot transfer by comparing spatially corresponding features and using self-supervision to preserve broadly useful information.

paragraphs: This paper presents a way to add provable adversarial robustness to an existing image classifier without changing the pretrained classifier itself. That makes the approach relevant to both locally available models and externally provided classification services. The protected system is a new classifier built around the existing one.

The method places a custom-trained denoiser before the classifier and combines this pipeline with randomized smoothing. Together, these components provide a mathematical robustness guarantee against adversarial perturbations measured using an l_p norm. The construction applies in both white-box settings, where the classifier is accessible internally, and black-box settings, where access is through its outputs.

The authors evaluate denoised smoothing on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 and demonstrate provable defenses for Azure, Google, AWS, and ClarifAI classification APIs. These experiments show how the construction can work with already deployed services. Its central practical contribution is separating the addition of certified robustness from retraining or modifying the underlying classifier, while still requiring a denoiser trained for the defense.
neurips-2020-denoised-smoothing-a-provab.tldr: Denoised smoothing adds provable adversarial robustness around pretrained image classifiers using a trained denoiser and randomized smoothing.

paragraphs: Discovering a causal graph involves deciding which variables directly influence others while avoiding directed cycles. The search is combinatorial, and the available data may not uniquely determine the correct graph. This paper builds on methods that turn graph discovery into continuous constrained optimization, bringing interventional data into that framework.

Interventions provide information about what happens when a system is actively changed, which can reduce ambiguity about causal relationships. The proposed method uses neural networks and has a theoretical foundation. It also demonstrates that expressive architectures, including normalizing flows, can fit within the continuous optimization formulation, extending the kinds of models that the framework can accommodate.

The authors report favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches across several intervention settings. These include perfect and imperfect interventions, as well as cases where the affected variables are unknown. The significance is the combination of flexible modeling and intervention-aware causal discovery. The abstract describes interventions as alleviating identifiability problems; it does not claim that they make every causal graph uniquely recoverable.
neurips-2020-differentiable-causal-disco.tldr: A neural continuous-optimization method uses interventional data to improve causal graph discovery across several intervention settings.

paragraphs: A nearest-neighbor classifier predicts a label from the labels of nearby observations. Choosing how many neighbors to use and how to weight them controls a trade-off between bias and variability. This paper develops a multiscale approach that combines information from several neighborhood sizes to improve how quickly classification error decreases with more data.

The method first forms ordinary unweighted nearest-neighbor estimates for several positive values of k. It then extrapolates those estimates toward k = 0. This imaginary zero-neighbor estimate is a mathematical extrapolation, rather than a prediction made without observations. The procedure implicitly produces real-valued weights that adapt to the query and its neighboring points.

Allowing negative weights matters because the abstract identifies them as essential for eliminating bias terms and reaching the optimal convergence rate. The authors prove an improved rate for their multiscale estimator, matching an existing optimal rate under certain conditions. The contribution is therefore a way to obtain adaptive weighting through extrapolation, together with a conditional theoretical improvement in excess-risk convergence.
neurips-2020-extrapolation-towards-imagi.tldr: Multiscale nearest-neighbor classification extrapolates toward an imaginary zero-neighbor estimate and attains an improved convergence rate under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Generating a molecule or a program is harder when the result must satisfy particular properties. This paper studies conditional generative models that directly map desired properties to a distribution over discrete structures. The challenge is that ordinary maximum-likelihood training can produce outputs that do not adequately respect the properties supplied as input.

The authors instead optimize an expected-reward objective, aligning training with how well generated structures meet the goal. They estimate model gradients by sampling from an approximation to normalized rewards. This permits simple Monte Carlo estimation while avoiding the high-variance score-function estimators that would otherwise be needed for the chosen reinforcement-learning objective.

The method is evaluated on molecules with user-specified properties and short Python expressions that must evaluate to a target value. It improves over maximum-likelihood training and other compared methods on both tasks. These findings support reward-oriented training as a way to strengthen the connection between a conditioning request and the resulting discrete output, without establishing that every generated structure will satisfy its requested constraints.
neurips-2020-goal-directed-generation-of.tldr: Reward-based training improves conditional generation of molecules and short programs by more directly targeting requested output properties.

paragraphs: Contrastive image learning brings representations of two augmented views of one image together while separating representations of different images. The negative examples determine what distinctions the model must learn. This paper investigates the importance of hard negatives: examples that pose a more challenging comparison than easily separated alternatives.

Existing approaches obtain useful negatives through large batches or large memory banks, but the abstract notes diminishing performance returns as memory requirements grow. The authors first find evidence within a strong contrastive framework that harder negatives can support better and faster learning. They then introduce feature-level mixing strategies that construct hard negatives during training with minimal additional computation.

The evaluation examines linear classification, object detection, and instance segmentation, including extensive ablations of the proposed approach. Adding hard negative mixing improves the representations learned by the studied state-of-the-art self-supervised method. The findings point to the content and difficulty of negative examples as an important design choice, alongside the number of negatives a training system can store or process.
neurips-2020-hard-negative-mixing-for-co.tldr: Mixing features to create harder negative examples improves contrastive visual representations with minimal computational overhead.

paragraphs: A contextual policy chooses actions or system settings according to the situation. Optimizing such a policy becomes difficult when feedback reports only an overall reward across many contexts. The learner sees whether the complete policy worked well, but cannot directly observe how well it performed in each individual context.

This paper develops Bayesian optimization models for that aggregate-feedback setting. The models use structure in the policy search space to make a high-dimensional optimization problem more manageable. Rather than requiring context-specific rewards, the approach searches over contextual policies using the aggregate outcomes that are actually available, addressing a measurement constraint that can arise in randomized trials and A/B tests.

Simulation studies compare the models' performance and robustness. Among the approaches studied, inferring a low-dimensional embedding of context performs best. The authors also demonstrate successful optimization of a real-world video bitrate policy. Together, these results support learning a compact representation of context as a useful way to optimize differentiated actions when evaluation only supplies a combined measure of success.
neurips-2020-high-dimensional-contextual.tldr: Structured Bayesian optimization learns contextual policies from aggregate rewards, with inferred low-dimensional context embeddings performing best in the reported simulations.

paragraphs: This paper places an energy-based model in the latent space of a generator. The energy model supplies a learned prior over latent vectors, while the generator maps those vectors into data. The two parts work together: one models which latent configurations are plausible, and the other expresses those configurations as outputs.

Both components are trained jointly by maximum likelihood. Training uses short runs of Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling from the latent prior and posterior distributions. Working in the lower-dimensional latent space is central to the approach: the authors argue that a simple energy model can capture useful regularities when paired with an expressive generator, while latent-space sampling remains efficient and mixes well.

The learned model shows strong performance on image generation, text generation, and anomaly detection in the reported evaluations. These applications illustrate how the same learned latent prior can support both producing data and identifying unusual observations. The contribution is a compact division of modeling work between an energy-based prior and a top-down generator, with a joint learning procedure connecting them.
neurips-2020-learning-latent-space-energ.tldr: A jointly learned energy-based latent prior and generator achieve strong reported results in generation and anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Style-based generators provide control over image synthesis, but their controls may not separate fine-grained semantic attributes. SariGAN addresses that problem by connecting latent factors to the meanings carried by feature channels. The aim is to make changes correspond more cleanly to particular visual properties within an image.

The model learns to group feature channels according to semantics and combines latent codes with channels at both channel and group levels. Adaptive group-wise normalization then controls the styles of different groups independently. The abstract illustrates this with changing whether a face's mouth is open while preserving other facial features, showing the intended level of localized semantic control.

Training jointly uses adversarial, channel-grouping, and mutual-information losses. The reported experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art style-based approaches in unconditional generation and conditional image inpainting, alongside high-fidelity synthesis and improved interpretability. The contribution links image quality with the organization of internal features: learned semantic groups become a mechanism for controlling distinct aspects of the generated image.
neurips-2020-learning-semantic-aware-nor.tldr: SariGAN groups feature channels by semantics and controls their normalization to produce more interpretable, fine-grained image edits.

paragraphs: Text-guided image manipulation requires a model to connect words with specific visual attributes, change the requested content, and preserve the rest. This paper proposes a lightweight generative adversarial network for that task. Its main design choice is to make training feedback more precise at the level of individual words.

A word-level discriminator supplies the generator with detailed signals about how image attributes relate to the description. This feedback helps a generator with relatively few parameters focus on the relevant attributes and edit them without affecting content absent from the text. Because the training signal explicitly concerns individual words, the discriminator can also use a simplified, lightweight structure.

Experiments show competitive manipulation performance with substantially fewer parameters than the compared state-of-the-art approach. They also indicate better separation of visual attributes and more accurate mapping between those attributes and corresponding words. The contribution connects efficiency with supervision granularity: targeted feedback supports smaller networks while helping the system make the particular modifications a description requests.
neurips-2020-lightweight-generative-adve.tldr: Word-level discriminator feedback enables smaller adversarial networks to make accurate text-guided image edits with competitive performance.

paragraphs: This paper extends approximate proximal-point methods to optimization updates that use minibatches of observations. The setting is stochastic convex optimization, and the broader method family includes stochastic subgradient, proximal-point, and bundle methods. The central question is how combining multiple observations per update changes convergence and practical behavior.

The authors propose two minibatch algorithms and prove finite-time convergence bounds that reveal a linear speedup with minibatch size. Unlike standard stochastic gradient methods, these methods may obtain that speedup even for nonsmooth objectives. They also retain a characteristic benefit of the approximate proximal-point family: robustness to the initial choice of step size.

For interpolation problems, the paper derives improved convergence rates and identifies a new way to parallelize alternating projections. Extensive experiments support the gains from accurate modeling and minibatching. The contribution therefore concerns both the amount of progress each update can make and how optimization can benefit from processing data together, with the nonsmooth speedup stated as a possibility rather than an unconditional property of every objective.
neurips-2020-minibatch-stochastic-approx.tldr: Two minibatch approximate proximal-point algorithms provide convergence guarantees and can achieve linear minibatch speedups even for nonsmooth objectives.

paragraphs: A heterogeneous treatment effect describes how an intervention's effect varies with observed characteristics. This paper studies estimating that variation when the effect is a smooth difference between two baseline functions that are individually less smooth. That modeling choice allows the quantity of interest to have more regularity than either baseline considered separately.

The authors determine tight statistical limits on estimation as a function of covariate geometry, meaning the arrangement of the observed characteristics. They also analyze a two-stage nearest-neighbor estimator that discards observations with poor matching quality. This estimator is near minimax optimal: its worst-case estimation performance is close to the best achievable within the studied setting.

A further result characterizes the tight dependence on the density ratio without assuming that covariate densities stay bounded away from zero. This matters for the theory because it allows regions where observations become sparse. A new maximal inequality supports the analysis. Together, the results connect matching quality, data geometry, and distribution imbalance to the achievable accuracy of treatment-effect estimation.
neurips-2020-minimax-optimal-nonparametr.tldr: A two-stage nearest-neighbor estimator nearly attains tight statistical limits for smooth treatment-effect differences between less smooth baselines.

paragraphs: Ensembles combine predictions from multiple models, but their memory and computation requirements grow with the number of models. This paper instead combines neural-network parameters into a fused model. Before averaging parameters, it uses optimal transport to softly align neurons across networks, layer by layer, so that the averaging accounts for their correspondence.

The authors show that this alignment can enable knowledge transfer without retraining between networks trained on heterogeneous, non-identically distributed data. They also report substantial improvements over direct parameter averaging in both identically distributed and heterogeneous settings. These findings make alignment an important part of the fusion procedure, rather than treating parameter positions as automatically comparable.

With moderate fine-tuning, the fused networks can serve as efficient replacements for ensembles in the reported evaluations across convolutional networks, residual networks, and multilayer perceptrons. The method also provides a principled way to combine networks with different widths, which the authors explore for compression. The abstract distinguishes transfer without retraining from ensemble replacement with fine-tuning; these are separate demonstrated uses.
neurips-2020-model-fusion-via-optimal-tr.tldr: Optimal-transport neuron alignment enables effective parameter fusion, including transfer without retraining and ensemble replacement with moderate fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks a rewarding policy using only previously collected interactions. MOReL approaches this through a learned model of the environment. It first constructs a pessimistic Markov decision process from the historical dataset and then learns a near-optimal policy inside that constructed decision process.

The pessimism has a specific theoretical role: for any policy, its performance in the constructed model approximately lower-bounds its performance in the real environment. The model therefore provides a conservative surrogate for evaluating and learning policies. Optimizing within it is motivated by the relationship between modeled performance and real performance, rather than simply trusting a learned environment model without such a relationship.

The authors prove minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors and report results matching or exceeding state-of-the-art performance on widely used offline benchmarks. The framework is modular, separating model construction from policy learning. That organization allows improvements in components such as model learning or planning to contribute to improvements in offline reinforcement learning within the same overall approach.
neurips-2020-morel-model-based-offline-r.tldr: MOReL learns policies in a pessimistic environment model and achieves minimax-optimal offline learning up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled examples with examples whose labels are unavailable. Common approaches use one weight to balance the labeled and unlabeled losses, giving every unlabeled example the same relative importance. This paper asks whether training can benefit from assigning a separate weight to each unlabeled example.

With one adjustable weight per example, manual tuning is no longer practical. The authors instead update the weights using an influence-function-based algorithm. An influence function measures how dependent a model is on an individual training observation, supplying a way to reason about examples separately. To make this approach efficient, the paper introduces a fast approximation to the influence function.

The method outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches on semi-supervised image and language classification tasks. These results support replacing a single shared balance with learned example-specific contributions. The contribution combines that finer control over unlabeled data with an approximation that makes the weighting procedure practical, rather than leaving the additional weights as a large manual tuning problem.
neurips-2020-not-all-unlabeled-data-are-.tldr: An efficient influence-function approximation learns separate weights for unlabeled examples and improves semi-supervised image and language classification.

paragraphs: Separating an object's representation from its background can help recognition, editing, and visual concept learning. One-GORD tackles this separation with only one annotated example per object category, together with unannotated images. The goal is to reduce annotation requirements while still handling the complicated backgrounds found in natural scenes.

The method augments each annotated example to create synthetic samples that guide the separation of object and background features. It then applies two self-supervised mechanisms, called dual-swapping and fuzzy classification, to the unannotated images. These mechanisms use the annotated example's guidance to learn the separation from a larger pool of images without requiring annotations for each one.

The authors also introduce two evaluation metrics, one addressing the learned representation and the other addressing images. Experiments show competitive separation performance and demonstrate operation on natural scenes with complex backgrounds. The stated annotation requirement is one sample for each category, so the result concerns learning with sparse category-specific guidance rather than learning without annotated examples.
neurips-2020-one-sample-guided-object-re.tldr: One-GORD uses one annotated example per category to guide separation of object and background features in unannotated natural images.

paragraphs: A simulated humanoid may be unable to reproduce recorded human motion because its dynamics differ from those of the person being imitated. Residual force control addresses that mismatch by adding external forces to the actions available to a reinforcement-learning controller. During training, the policy learns how to use those forces to better follow reference motion.

Experiments across dynamic motions show faster convergence and higher-quality learned motion than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The demonstrations include agile ballet movements such as pirouettes, arabesques, and jetés. The extra forces are central to the approach: they compensate for a mismatch that could otherwise make the human reference physically unattainable for the simulated model.

The paper also combines a kinematic policy with an RFC-based policy to generate diverse motions over an unlimited horizon without task guidance or user input. The authors report learning from Human3.6M and generating varied long-term behavior. This extends the contribution from imitating individual demanding skills to coordinating motion generation and physical control across continuing sequences.
neurips-2020-residual-force-control-for-.tldr: Learned external residual forces help simulated humanoids imitate agile human motion and support diverse long-term motion synthesis.

paragraphs: Persistence diagrams summarize geometric and topological features that appear across multiple scales in data. Their usefulness can be undermined by sensitivity to perturbations in the input. This paper constructs diagrams through robust density estimation, aiming to reduce the effect of outliers on the resulting topological summary.

The framework uses reproducing kernels to build robust density estimators, then forms superlevel filtrations by examining regions above varying density thresholds. An analogue of the influence function measures sensitivity in the space of persistence diagrams. Using this tool, the authors establish that their construction is less sensitive to outliers, giving a statistical basis for the robustness claim.

The paper also proves consistency in bottleneck distance, a measure of discrepancy between persistence diagrams. Kernel smoothness controls the convergence rate, and the analysis supports uniform confidence bands in diagram space. Benchmark experiments demonstrate improved performance. Together, the results address robustness, convergence, and uncertainty, turning the construction into a statistically characterized method for extracting topological features.
neurips-2020-robust-persistence-diagrams.tldr: Kernel-based robust density estimates produce persistence diagrams with reduced outlier sensitivity, consistency guarantees, and confidence bands.

paragraphs: Large public weather archives contain valuable observations, but their scale and complexity make them difficult to use for training deep-learning systems. SEVIR organizes that material into a curated dataset of more than 10,000 weather events. Each event contains image sequences covering a 384-by-384-kilometer area over four hours.

The dataset aligns observations in both space and time across five data types: three GOES-16 satellite imagery channels, NEXRAD vertically integrated liquid mosaics, and GOES-16 lightning observations. This alignment lets researchers work with corresponding views of the same event from different sensors. Many events are also matched to NOAA storm records, allowing imagery to be linked with descriptions and reported impacts.

The paper explains the collection methodology and demonstrates uses in precipitation nowcasting and synthetic weather radar generation. It also supplies baseline implementations and describes evaluation metrics. Its contribution is shared research infrastructure: coordinated observations, event information, and example modeling workflows that make weather imagery more accessible for developing and evaluating new learning methods.
neurips-2020-sevir-a-storm-event-imagery.tldr: SEVIR provides aligned multisensor imagery for over 10,000 weather events, with baseline models and evaluation tools for meteorological learning.

paragraphs: Graph-learning methods based on one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman processing can miss patterns involving richer interactions among vertices. Higher-dimensional versions consider tuples of vertices, capturing higher-order structure but introducing scaling problems and possible overfitting. This paper develops local variants intended to make that richer processing more practical.

The proposed algorithms consider only part of the original neighborhood of each vertex tuple, and the authors construct corresponding neural architectures. Restricting these neighborhoods reduces computation and susceptibility to overfitting. The paper also establishes that one proposed algorithm has strictly greater power than the original algorithm for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, showing that the local construction can retain substantial representational strength.

Experiments report sharply reduced computation times and prevention of overfitting in the evaluated settings for both kernel and neural versions. The kernel method achieves state-of-the-art graph classification results across a broad collection of benchmarks, while the neural version shows promising results on large-scale molecular regression. The contribution combines higher-order graph representations with a more selective computational structure.
neurips-2020-weisfeiler-and-leman-go-spa.tldr: Local higher-order Weisfeiler–Leman methods reduce computation and overfitting while supporting expressive graph kernels and neural architectures.
